entry.title: Some thoughts on AI and Education

link.title: Some thoughts on AI and Education

entry.content:
A New Tool for Education

I spend my working life around supercomputers. One thing you learn fast in that world is that a new one doesn’t just let you run your code faster. It changes which questions are worth asking in the first place. Generative AI looks like that kind of enabler, and it has landed in the classroom whether or not any of us feel ready for it.

It’s not the first time a tool like this has shown up in a classroom. When the handheld calculator landed in the 1970s, plenty of teachers called it cheating. Why would a kid bother learning long division if the answer was a button press away. That worry wasn’t unreasonable at the time. What actually happened was less dramatic and more useful. The calculator did the arithmetic, which meant students could spend the same hour going further: working bigger and more challenging problems, checking whether an answer was even plausible, setting up the question in the first place. It wasn’t a shortcut around thinking. It was an amplifier. I suspect AI is going to follow the same arc, only on a much larger scale and on a much faster clock.

I want to be even-handed here, because I think the honest position is an uncomfortable one. AI in education carries real promise and real hazard, often inside the very same feature. So instead of reaching for a verdict, I want to work through the two questions I keep being asked: what is the role for students, and what is the role for faculty. I’ll take them in order.

The role for students

The most valuable thing AI offers a student, to my mind, is not answers. It is a way to explore. A capable model is a tireless companion for poking at an idea. What happens if I change this assumption. What would the strongest counterargument be. Where did this concept come from, and what am I not seeing. In the lab we’d call this the exploratory phase of a problem, the stretch of work before you even know what the real question is. Students have always had to do that phase mostly alone. They no longer do, and that is a genuine gain.

Close behind exploration is the role of tutor. A student stuck at eleven at night on a problem set now has something patient to ask. It will explain the same proof three different ways. It will not sigh. For a student who never had a parent who knew calculus, or a family that could afford a tutor, that is not a small thing. Used this way, AI can be a real leveler.

It is also a drafting and feedback tool, and here I’d ask for a little more care. Used well, it helps you get unstuck on a blank page and gives you a fast read on whether an argument actually holds together. Used poorly, it simply writes the thing, and you hand in work you could not have produced and do not fully understand.

That points straight at the hazard, and the hazard is real. The same tool that can accelerate a student’s thinking can also quietly stand in for it. If the slow, frustrating work of wrestling with a hard problem is the thing that actually builds a mind, then a tool that removes the wrestling can remove the education along with it. The fluent answer arrives, the struggle gets skipped, and something important fails to happen. No syllabus policy fully fixes this. It comes down to whether a student understands what the work is for, and teaching that understanding is partly our job. Which is a fair place to turn to the second question.

The role for faculty

For faculty, the most immediate benefit is mundane, and I think badly underrated: time. A great deal of academic life is not teaching and not discovery. It is drafting, summarizing, reformatting, wrangling logistics, and writing the same category of email for the hundredth time. AI is genuinely good at that kind of work. Every hour it hands back is an hour that can go to a student, a problem, or a piece of writing that truly needs a human mind. I’ve watched the same pattern in research computing for years. When the tool handles the boilerplate, the scientist gets to spend attention on the part that is actually hard.

The deeper opportunity, and the harder one, is rethinking courses and assessment. If a take-home essay can be generated in seconds, then the take-home essay is no longer measuring what we assumed it measured. That is uncomfortable, but it is also clarifying. It forces us to ask what we were really trying to assess, and then to design for that directly: a defense of an idea out loud, work shown in stages, problems that reward judgment over recall. This is more work for faculty in the near term. It is also, I’d argue, overdue.

AI can serve as a teaching aid in its own right. It can generate practice problems without end, adapt an explanation to a confused student in real time, and let a whole class examine where a model fails as a lesson in itself. Some of the best classroom uses I’ve seen treat the AI as the object of study rather than the oracle. Here is what it got wrong. Why do you think that happened. How would you check.

The hazard for faculty mirrors the one for students. Under time pressure, it is easy to let the tool lower the bar without noticing: to grade carelessly with it, to teach from material we never properly vetted, to stop catching the moments when rigor has slipped. The tool does not protect rigor. Only we do.

What does not change

Here is what I keep returning to. When the student and the professor have the same powerful tool sitting on the desk, the old picture of the faculty member as the holder and dispenser of information is finished. That picture was already fading. AI ends it. What remains is, I think, the better part of the job anyway. Education was never really about the transfer of facts. It was about building judgment: the ability to frame a good question, to tell a sound answer from a plausible-sounding wrong one, to know what actually matters. A national lab runs on precisely those skills, because a supercomputer will faithfully return a precise answer to a badly posed question. The tool is only ever as good as the mind directing it.

So the role for students is to use AI to think harder, not less. The role for faculty is to model what thinking harder looks like, and to build an education that AI can assist but cannot counterfeit. The promise is real and the pitfalls are real, and I don’t believe we get to choose just one. We have a new tool in the classroom. The question worth asking has not changed: what are we actually trying to teach.
entry.summary: On AI as a new tool in the classroom, what it changes for students and for faculty, and what stays true about teaching when one sits on every desk.

entry.title: The Long and Winding Road
entry.content:
There’s a sentence I’ve waited years to write, so I’m going to write it carefully. The Department of Energy’s Aurora supercomputer has entered production at the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility, and the exascale system is now open to the broader research community.

If you don’t work in this corner of the field, that may read as a routine announcement. A machine was built; the machine was switched on. I’d like to gently push back on that, because Aurora was never routine, and the road that led here was neither short nor straight.

Here are the facts I’m proud of. Aurora was built in partnership with Intel and Hewlett Packard Enterprise. It integrates roughly 60,000 Intel Data Center GPU Max Series accelerators across its 10,000 nodes, and it now stands as the second U.S. exascale system available to open science, alongside Oak Ridge’s Frontier. Those are genuinely staggering numbers. But numbers have a way of hiding the years behind them, and it’s the years I want to talk about.

A system like this does not simply arrive. It is coaxed into existence. There were several years of system bring-up, of scaling tests, of Early Science Program campaigns that pushed the machine in ways its earliest plans never anticipated. There were long stretches where progress was measured in small, unglamorous increments, and stretches where the most honest status update we could give was “not yet.” Anyone who has built something genuinely hard knows that particular feeling: the milestone keeps receding, and you keep walking toward it anyway. Aurora asked that of a lot of people for a long time.

This next part is the one I most want to get right, because it’s the part that doesn’t fit in a press release. The reason Aurora got here is not a vendor and not a budget line. It’s a team. It’s people who showed up through the uncertainty, who debugged at scale when the scale itself was the problem, who learned to treat each setback as information rather than as defeat. I have the enormous privilege of working alongside them, and I want to be plain about my own part in it: mostly, I got to watch extraordinary people refuse to give up. A facility is not its hardware. It is the patience and the stubbornness and the plain care of the people who run it. I have never been more certain of that than I am this week.

So what happens now. Allocations on Aurora, including those awarded through INCITE, ALCC, and the ALCF Director’s Discretionary program, move into routine production use. The system will carry a portfolio of science campaigns spanning materials, climate, fusion, drug discovery, cosmology, and frontier AI. Researchers who have waited their turn now get the machine. That is the entire point of the long road. We didn’t build Aurora in order to have built Aurora. We built it so that someone, somewhere, can ask a question that was previously unaskable and actually get an answer back.

And so, for our deployment team, the production milestone is the start of the story rather than the end of it. The hard, ordinary, beautiful work of science begins. The road was long and it was winding, and I would not trade the people I walked it with for anything. Coverage of the milestone is available at HPCwire.
entry.summary: The Department of Energy's Aurora supercomputer enters full production at the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility, opening to the broader research community.

entry.title: Coming Home to a Special Place

link.title: Coming Home to a Special Place

entry.content:
The University of Illinois Chicago has appointed me the fifth Director of the Electronic Visualization Laboratory (EVL). I’ve found myself thinking less about the title than about the place, so the place is what I want to write about.

For anyone who hasn’t crossed paths with it, EVL is a hard place to summarize. It was founded in 1973 by computer scientist Tom DeFanti and artist-physicist Dan Sandin as a joint program of the College of Engineering and the School of Art and Design. That pairing was unusual then and, frankly, it’s still unusual now. Most labs pick a side. EVL never did. It has spent more than fifty years sitting squarely in the space where computing, visualization, and the arts overlap, which makes it one of the longest-running interdisciplinary research labs anywhere. EVL is probably best known for conceiving and building the CAVE virtual reality theater in 1991, a room you could walk into and be surrounded by a simulation, years before “immersive” became a marketing word.

I mention the CAVE for a reason that isn’t about institutional history. I worked on it (or maybe I should say in it) as a graduate student. That project, in that lab, is where my career actually began.

I came to EVL young and unformed, and the lab handed me something I didn’t know I needed: a workbench shared with people who thought nothing like me. Artists who cared about how a thing felt and looked. Engineers who cared about whether the thing would hold up under load. Scientists who just wanted to see their data. The thought-provoking conversations and the collaboration across that mix of people taught me more than any single course ever did. I went on to earn a master’s degree from UIC in 1994, and I joined UIC’s computer science faculty in 2022. But the through-line of all of it traces back to a graduate student standing inside a glowing cube, trying to make a picture move correctly.

EVL is also, quietly, the reason I have spent 30-plus years at Argonne National Laboratory. A national lab is an interdisciplinary instrument by design. It only works when physicists, computer scientists, mathematicians, and engineers can sit at the same table and actually hear one another. I walked into Argonne already fluent in that, because EVL had taught me the language of collaboration and being part of a team. I didn’t have to learn how to collaborate across a divide; I had simply never worked any other way. That fluency turned out to be the single most useful thing I brought with me, and EVL is where it came from.

So a few words on how I think about leading, because stepping into a director’s role forces you to put it into sentences.

I don’t believe the best ideas come from the front of the room. They come from the room. My job, as I understand it, is not to be the smartest voice but to keep the right people in conversation long enough for something unexpected to happen, and then to get out of the way of it. Interdisciplinary work is slow and occasionally maddening, because two specialists often can’t even agree on what the problem is before they can solve it. A leader’s real task is to protect that messy middle stretch, to make it safe to be confused out loud, and to resist the urge to flatten everything into a single discipline’s language just because that would be tidier. EVL has done this for half a century. My role isn’t to fix it or to steer it. It’s to make sure the environment stays in place, so the people here have the room to do their work.

The original EVL vision, that computing and the arts and the sciences belong together, feels less like a historical curiosity and more like an urgent idea. As our tools get more powerful, the hard questions are increasingly about meaning, perception, and human judgment, and those are exactly the questions you can’t answer from inside one field. Interdisciplinary research is more important now than it has ever been.

I owe this place a great deal. It shaped my career, led me to Argonne, and taught me how to work with people who don’t share my training. The best thing I can do now is help keep it the kind of place that does the same for the next person who walks in.
entry.summary: The University of Illinois Chicago has named me the fifth Director of the Electronic Visualization Laboratory, the interdisciplinary research lab that produced the original CAVE virtual reality system.

entry.title: Worlds Colliding at the Lab
entry.content:
Argonne hosts a lot of visitors. Cabinet secretaries, members of Congress, graduate students, journalists, schoolkids, foreign delegations, the occasional Nobel laureate. After more than a few years here you stop being surprised by who shows up. Earlier this week we hosted Darryl Jones, bassist for The Rolling Stones, ahead of the band’s Chicago tour stop. As best as I can recall, he was the first rock star.

Music has always been a big part of my life. I’ve been to hundreds of shows over the years, all kinds of venues, all kinds of scenes. Chicago is the right city for it. Every summer there’s Pitchfork, Riot Fest, and Lollapalooza, and I make a point of going to each when I can. I can no longer do multi-day festivals at my age, but I still pick a day as often as possible.

So when the call came in asking if I could host a VIP tour for Darryl Jones, I had to stop and ask who that was. I like the Stones, don’t get me wrong. I just had not been paying attention to who took over from Bill Wyman.

He showed up with real questions, and a lot of them. How Aurora actually works. What we run on it. Why the science matters. The tour ran long because the conversation kept going. That is the kind of tour I enjoy giving.

That night I caught the show. It was one of the best concerts I have ever seen, and given my count, that is saying something. Watching a man play to a stadium after spending the afternoon walking him through climate models is a particular kind of jolt. The thoughtful, curious person in the Aurora aisles and the bass player onstage were the same person, which is obvious in hindsight but still strange to witness.

That is what I keep coming back to. Most of the people who visit a place like Argonne come for the science, and most of the tour is a science conversation. But every once in a while a visit also brushes up against the rest of your life. The lab side of me and the music side of me had been politely ignoring each other for decades. For one afternoon, and then one very loud evening, they got to sit in the same room.
entry.summary: On hosting Rolling Stones bassist Darryl Jones at Aurora, a lifetime of shows and festivals, and what happens when the music half of your life and the science half finally share a hallway.

entry.title: Building an instrument other people get to use

link.title: Building an instrument other people get to use

entry.content:
Some of the most useful research infrastructure isn’t built by the people who eventually use it. Telescopes, particle accelerators, light sources, supercomputers, sensor networks: each one is a piece of capability that took years to design and stand up, and the science it enables comes from researchers who arrive after the work is done. The instrument is what the previous generation hands the next.

That framing is what I keep returning to when I look at this new NSF testbed grant. The award funds the design and construction of A National-Scale Testbed Supporting Artificial Intelligence Research Spanning the Computing Continuum. Pete Beckman is principal investigator, leading from Northwestern, and I’m a co-PI alongside Ilkay Altintas, Eugene Kelly, and Nicola Ferrier. The $3.2M is the line in the press release. The thing that matters is what the line buys.

What the line buys is a continuation. The testbed builds on years of work with the Array of Things, and the Sage cyberinfrastructure that grew out of it, into something larger and open to a much wider set of researchers. The point of opening it is straightforward. The kind of distributed AI research the award envisions, where edge sensors, regional infrastructure, and centralized supercomputers are treated as one continuum, is something you cannot do without scale. Most groups don’t have that scale. A shared testbed gives it to them.

Democratizing access is the part I keep coming back to. There are AI questions worth asking that come from researchers who don’t sit next door to a leadership-class facility, and they shouldn’t have to relocate to ask them. A national testbed is a way of saying: the instrument exists, you have a key, go.

Award details are at the NSF award page.
entry.summary: On testbeds as research instruments, the Array of Things lineage, and democratizing access to the computing continuum.

entry.title: Why visualization still matters in the age of AI

link.title: Why visualization still matters in the age of AI

entry.content:
It is fashionable, at the moment, to assume that AI will eat every step of the scientific pipeline. Generate the candidates, score the candidates, pick the winner, write the paper. I don’t think the middle of that sentence holds up under examination. At some point a person still has to look at the result, decide what it means, share it with a colleague, and figure out the next move. That step is not going away, and it is not the part the model is good at.

Which is why visualization, the unglamorous part, still matters. When an AI-driven drug discovery pipeline produces hundreds of thousands of candidate molecules, you cannot read them. You cannot make a spreadsheet of them. The number of candidates is the entire problem. What you need is a way to see the structure of the space, find the regions worth attention, and hand the interesting bits to a chemist who knows what to do with them. Without that step, the candidates may as well not exist.

ChemoGraph, the paper our team had recognized at EuroVis 2023 with an Honorable Mention in the Best Paper category, is a clean example of that point. The work was led by Bharat Kale, then finishing his PhD, and was the core of his dissertation. The team included Austin Clyde, Maoyuan Sun, Arvind Ramanathan, Rick Stevens, and me. It was largely an Argonne effort, anchored in the lab’s COVID-19 drug screening campaigns, and built to make those screenings legible to the people doing the screening.

The award is great, and Bharat earned it. The reason the project is worth talking about beyond the award is that it sits at the seam where AI hands off to humans. As long as that seam exists, and I don’t think it’s going anywhere soon, visualization is doing real work in the pipeline, not decorating it.

The paper is published in Computer Graphics Forum and is available at Wiley Online Library.
entry.summary: On the part of the pipeline a model can't do for you. Even when AI generates more candidates than any person can read, someone still has to look, share, and decide.

entry.title: There is a national lab twenty-two miles from Chicago

link.title: There is a national lab twenty-two miles from Chicago

entry.content:
There is a national laboratory twenty-two miles outside Chicago doing some of the most interesting computing in the world, and most Chicagoans haven’t heard of it. This is the part I keep coming back to. Argonne sits a short drive from the Loop, the work happening there is paid for by the public, and the public mostly doesn’t know it’s there. That gap is on us, not on them.

The default way to talk about a system like Aurora is to talk about it in the trade press. HPCwire, Inside HPC, the conference circuit. Those venues matter, but the audience is already in the room. They know what an exascale machine is. They know which lab is which. Writing for them is necessary, but it isn’t outreach, it’s part of the job.

Which is why a piece like the one Chicago Magazine ran was worth the time. A long-form profile in a city magazine reaches a different audience. People who live here, ride past the lab on I-55 without thinking about it, and have no particular reason to read the trade press. If even a few of them come away knowing that Aurora exists and that it’s in their backyard, the piece did its job.

The article, The Computer That Will Change Everything, ran as the February 2023 cover feature. I’m fine with the headline. Aurora at the time was the fastest machine in the world for AI, and breathless framing isn’t always wrong. The interview process itself was unlike any I’d had before, with a photo shoot fun as we looked for unusual places to take pictures.

The full feature is at Chicago Magazine.
entry.summary: On who advanced computing is for, why a city magazine feature mattered more than another trade-press piece, and what it means that most Chicagoans haven't heard of Argonne.

entry.title: A step back into physics, by way of computing

link.title: A step back into physics, by way of computing

entry.content:
People sometimes describe high-energy physics as a step away from my main work. From where I’m standing it’s the opposite. My undergraduate degree was in physics at NIU. I spent three summers at Fermilab during those years, and I started graduate school in physics before computing pulled me in another direction. So a project that sits between computer science and experimental particle physics isn’t unfamiliar territory. It’s territory I started in.

Careers don’t always go in straight lines, and the parts I’ve enjoyed most have almost always been the interdisciplinary ones. Pure single-field work has its rewards, but the interesting questions, in my experience, tend to live in the overlaps. Particle physics needs serious computing to function. Computing benefits from being pointed at problems that don’t bend. Putting students inside both at once, before they’ve decided which side they belong on, seems like the right thing to do.

The new DOE training grant we picked up does exactly that. The program, Chicagoland Computational Traineeship in High Energy Particle Physics (C2-the-P2), is a $2.6M, five-year award led by NIU particle physicist Jahred Adelman, with NIU co-investigators Vishnu Zutshi, Jerry Blazey, and Mike Eads. On the UIC side I’m working with Rick Cavanaugh, who brings the physics expertise. Trainees work alongside researchers at Argonne and Fermilab, which lands me back in a building I haven’t worked in since I was an undergraduate.

What I appreciate about how the program is built is that the funding goes where it should. “The great thing about this grant is that the overwhelming majority of the funding goes directly to students,” Adelman noted, with stipends and tuition reimbursement built in. Training programs work or fail on whether the students can afford to take part, and this one is structured so they can.

More information is at the program website and the NIU news release.
entry.summary: On interdisciplinary work, the way careers loop back to old interests, and a DOE training grant that lands me close to where I started.

entry.title: What science looks like when the silos come down

link.title: What science looks like when the silos come down

entry.content:
For most of my career, simulation lived in one building, data analysis lived in another, and AI lived somewhere down the road, mostly in computer science departments. People moved between them, but the methods didn’t, not really. You did one of the three and borrowed the others when you had to.

That arrangement is coming apart. The interesting science problems now want all three at once, in the same workflow, on the same machine, often inside the same job. Not because anyone declared it should be that way, but because the problems don’t sit cleanly inside any one of the categories anymore. The boundary between training a model, running a simulation, and analyzing the result is getting fuzzy enough that drawing it isn’t useful.

The GenSLMs project is a good example, which is part of why it’s worth talking about. The team trained genome-scale language models on raw nucleotide sequences to track how SARS-CoV-2 was evolving. Biology, language models, and leadership-class computing in one pipeline. My role was on the ALCF side, helping to enable the runs. The 2022 ACM Gordon Bell Special Prize for COVID-19 Research, announced at SC22 in Dallas, recognized the work, and the team behind it across Argonne, the University of Chicago, NVIDIA, Cerebras, UIC, Caltech, Harvard, NIU, the Technical University of Munich, and the ALCF.

The reason the prize matters more than the usual press release is that it’s the community putting the new shape on the record. A Gordon Bell isn’t given for projects that look like everything else; it’s given for projects that look like where things are going. That this one combined simulation, data, and AI on a single problem, and won, says something about which direction the wind is blowing. The next decade is going to look more like this and less like the one before it.

Coverage of the award is at Inside HPC.
entry.summary: On the next decade of computational science, where simulation, data, and AI stop living in separate buildings, and what a Gordon Bell prize signals about that direction.

entry.title: Teaching the systems by letting students touch them

link.title: Teaching the systems by letting students touch them

entry.content:
You can lecture about a cloud testbed for a semester and end up with a room full of students who can describe one but have never used one. That gap is the part of teaching computing that has bothered me for a long time. The technology moves quickly, the syllabus moves slowly, and the distance between the two is mostly closed by hand-waving at slides.

The way out, as far as I can tell, is to put the actual systems in front of students. Not a screenshot of the system, the system. Cloud testbeds and notebooks make that more possible than it used to be. A notebook can hold the explanation and the runnable thing in the same artifact, so the student stops being an audience and starts being an operator. A testbed like Chameleon, which Kate Keahey runs out of Argonne and the University of Chicago, gives them real infrastructure to operate on, not a sandbox that pretends.

That’s the bet underneath the new NSF CyberTraining award we picked up this summer, where I’m a co-PI on the NIU side with Dave Koop, in collaboration with Kate’s group. The funded work is about course material that runs on Chameleon. The thing I actually care about is the pedagogical shift the funded work makes possible: less lecturing about data-centric computing, more doing it.

I don’t think this fully solves the gap. Pure lecture is hard to dislodge, and good hands-on material takes more work to build than slides do. But the direction is right. If we want students to be ready for the systems they’ll actually meet after graduation, those systems need to be close enough for them to touch.

Award details are at the NSF award listing.
entry.summary: On the limits of pure lecture mode for data systems and advanced computing, and what changes when students can actually run the thing.
